questions.knowledge_point: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting One Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $64$ as ${4}^{3},$ and then rewrite the left-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{k-1} & ={64}^{2k} \\ {4}^{k-1} & ={({4}^{3})}^{2k} \\ {4}^{k-1} & ={4}^{6k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(4),$ we equate the exponents and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k-1 & =6k \\ -1 & =5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the value of $d$ that satisfies the equation ${25}^{d-7}={625}^{d+10}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $25={5}^{2}$ and $625={5}^{4}$ as follows:

$$
{({5}^{2})}^{d-7}={({5}^{4})}^{d+10}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2(d-7)}={5}^{4(d+10)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(5)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $d:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(d-7) & =4(d+10) \\ 2d-14 & =4d+40 \\ -2d & =54 \\ d & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{({4}^{2})}^{b}={({4}^{3})}^{b+4}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2b}={4}^{3(b+4)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2b & =3(b+4) \\ 2b & =3b+12 \\ b & =-12\end{aligned}
